theory.what: Firewalls control traffic flow between network zones based on rules. They inspect packets and allow/deny based on source, destination, port, protocol, and state.
theory.why: Firewalls are the primary network security control. They enforce the principle of least privilege at the network level — only explicitly allowed traffic passes.
theory.how:
Types:
- Packet filter: Stateless, checks individual packets
- Stateful: Tracks connection state, allows return traffic
- NGFW: Adds application awareness, IPS, URL filtering

Rule processing: Top-down, first match wins. Implicit deny at bottom.
theory.when: Deploy firewalls at: internet edge, between security zones, in front of sensitive servers, between departments. Always default deny.
theory.configuration:
! Cisco ASA example
access-list OUTSIDE_IN permit tcp any host 203.0.113.10 eq 443
access-list OUTSIDE_IN deny ip any any log
!
access-group OUTSIDE_IN in interface outside

theory.what: IDS detects malicious activity and alerts. IPS detects AND blocks malicious activity inline. Both use signatures and anomaly detection.
theory.why: Firewalls allow/deny based on ports — they can't inspect payload content. IDS/IPS examines packet contents for exploit signatures, malware, and anomalous behavior.
theory.how:
Deployment:
- IDS: Passive (mirror/SPAN port) — detects and alerts only
- IPS: Inline — detects and blocks in real-time

Detection methods:
- Signature-based: Known attack patterns
- Anomaly-based: Deviations from baseline
- Policy-based: Violations of defined rules
theory.when: Deploy IDS/IPS at network boundaries, in front of critical servers, and between security zones. Use IPS inline for active protection, IDS for monitoring-only.
theory.configuration:
# Suricata IPS (inline)
suricata -c /etc/suricata/suricata.yaml -i eth0 --af-packet

# Snort IDS
snort -c /etc/snort/snort.conf -i eth0 -A alert_fast

theory.what: IPSec VPN creates encrypted tunnels between sites (site-to-site) or between remote users and the network (remote access). Provides confidentiality, integrity, and authentication.
theory.why: Data traversing the internet is vulnerable to interception. IPSec VPN encrypts all traffic between endpoints, creating a secure channel over untrusted networks.
theory.how:
IPSec phases:
Phase 1 (IKE): Authenticate peers, establish secure channel
- Main Mode or Aggressive Mode
- Negotiate: encryption, hash, DH group, auth method

Phase 2 (IPSec SA): Negotiate data encryption
- ESP (Encapsulating Security Payload): Encrypts + authenticates
- AH (Authentication Header): Authenticates only

Modes: Tunnel (entire packet encrypted) vs Transport (payload only).
theory.when: Use IPSec for: site-to-site connectivity over internet, remote access VPN, encrypting traffic between cloud and on-premises.
theory.configuration:
! Cisco Site-to-Site VPN
crypto isakmp policy 10
 encryption aes 256
 hash sha256
 authentication pre-share
 group 14
crypto isakmp key SECRET address 203.0.113.1
!
crypto ipsec transform-set AES-SHA esp-aes 256 esp-sha256-hmac
crypto map VPN 10 ipsec-isakmp
 set peer 203.0.113.1
 set transform-set AES-SHA
 match address VPN-TRAFFIC

theory.what: Network segmentation divides a network into isolated zones with controlled access between them. Each zone has its own security policy.
theory.why: Flat networks allow lateral movement — once an attacker gets in, they can reach everything. Segmentation limits blast radius and enforces least privilege at the network level.
theory.how:
Implementation methods:
- VLANs + inter-VLAN firewall rules
- Physical separation
- Microsegmentation (host-based)
- Zero Trust Network Access (ZTNA)

Common zones: DMZ, Internal, Management, Guest, IoT, PCI CDE.
theory.when: Segment when: you have different trust levels, compliance requirements (PCI CDE), IoT devices, guest access, or want to limit breach impact.
theory.configuration:
! Inter-VLAN firewall (on L3 switch or firewall)
access-list 101 permit tcp 10.0.10.0 0.0.0.255 10.0.20.0 0.0.0.255 eq 443
access-list 101 deny ip 10.0.10.0 0.0.0.255 10.0.20.0 0.0.0.255
access-list 101 permit ip any any
troubleshooting: Verify traffic is being filtered between zones
Review firewall logs for denied traffic

theory.what: 802.1X is a port-based network access control standard. Devices must authenticate before getting network access. Unauthenticated devices are blocked or placed in a guest VLAN.
theory.why: Without 802.1X, anyone who plugs into a network port gets access. 802.1X ensures only authorized devices and users can access the network — essential for zero trust.
theory.how:
Components:
- Supplicant: Client device requesting access
- Authenticator: Switch port enforcing access
- Authentication Server: RADIUS server (validates credentials)

Process: Device connects → switch challenges → device provides credentials → RADIUS validates → switch grants/denies access.
theory.when: Implement 802.1X on all access ports in secure environments. Use for: corporate wired access, wireless (WPA2-Enterprise), and IoT device authentication.
theory.configuration:
! Switch port 802.1X
aaa new-model
aaa authentication dot1x default group radius
!
interface GigabitEthernet0/1
 switchport mode access
 authentication port-control auto
 dot1x pae authenticator
 authentication host-mode multi-auth
